lawyer:
Abdul Malek with K. Z. Alam, Zamiruddin Ahmed ----- For the petitioner. 
M. Shorab Ali, D.A.G. with Hassan Ariff ----- For the Opposite party.
parties:
M. G Towab Air. Vice Marshal (Rtd) ----- Petitioner
Vs.
The State ----- Respondent
full_judgment:
4. The petitioner in his application before this Court has submitted that he was a Group Captain and the senior-most Bengali Officer in the then Pakistan Air Force till 1971 and resigned from the Pakistan Air Force when the war of liberation started. After liberation of the country, the then Prime Minister Mr. Sheikh Mujibur Rahman offered him the Chairmanship of the Bangladesh Biman but the petitioner upon an assessment of the position of the Organisation at that time expressed his inability to accept the offer. In 1975 the petitioner was called back home and was appointed the Chief of Air Staff, Bangladesh Air Force on 14.10.75. Thereafter the petitioner was appointed the DCMLA on 8.11.75 and was assigned the charges of various Minis-tries including Civil Aviation, Tourism, Food, Petroleum and Mineral Resources. As the DCMLA in charge of the Ministry of Civil Aviation, the Bangladesh Biman also came under his charge. The petitioner after giving details of the organisational and financial position of the I3iman at that time in his application came to the conclusion that the Biman had earned the reputation of being one of the most unreliable airlines in the world. The petitioner in the interest of the Biman and the country took several steps which earned him the wrath and enmity of certain vested interest in the Biman. The petitioner in his application and in his affidavit has given the details of the various stages of negotiation leading to the purchase of the aircraft in question. The petitioner was thereafter arbitrarily relieved of his office on 30.4.76 and was forced out of the country on the same day without being allowed to collect even his personal effects. The petitioner who is a Bangladeshi national tried to return to his country of origin on several occasions but was denied permission. He ultimately arrived at the Dacca Airport on 1.7.80 but was not allowed to come out of the Airport and was illegally detained there for about 8 hours and eventually forced out of the country again by the then Government at Government costs. The petitioner in his application goes on to submit that he moved this Court by way of a Writ Partition being Writ Petition No. 673 of 1980 and the action of the Government refusing the petitioner's entry into Bangladesh and the order of expulsion was declared illegal by this Court on 23.7.81. After the judgment the petitioner returned to Dacca from abroad on 21.8.81 but on the following morning he was arrested by the. Police in connection with the instant case which was instituted on 13.5.80 and was in custody for 5 days before he was released on bail by the Court. The petitioner then moved this Court and obtained the present Rule. 

 5. Mr. Abdul Malek, the learned Counsel appearing for the petitioner has taken us through the petition, the affidavit and the reply thereto and has argued that even on the admitted facts, no case under any law far less under section 5(2) of Act II of 1947 has been made out against the petitioner. He has further argued that the prosecution is wholly motivated, malafide and has been launched only to humiliate, harass and victimise the petitioner. The learned Deputy Attorney General appearing for the State has in reply submitted that the facts revealed in the F.I.R. bad enough ingredients to constitute an offence of criminal misconduct as laid down under section 5 of Act II of 1947, and that the petitioner purchased a different kind of aircraft contrary to the decision of the Government and thereby obtained wrongful gain by abusing his official position. The learned Deputy Attorney General has further argued that the quashing of the proceeding at this stage would amount to stifling of the proceeding by exercising the extraordinary powers vested in the Court. 

 9. So far as the second part of the charge relating to the obtaining of pecuniary advantage is concerned, it is necessary to consider the whole background leading to the impounding of the aircraft and consequent loss to the Biman and the country. It is pertinent to remember in this connection that when the aircraft in question was impounded in London the petitioner was already relieved of his responsibilities and was nowhere in the governmental hierarchy. We had in course of hearing of the Rule pointedly asked the learned Deputy Attorney General as to how they could arrive at the figure of dollar 6,36,000 in the charge against the petitioner. The learned Deputy Attorney General even after consulting the concerned officials could not give us any satisfactory reply. The allegation in the F.I.R. was that the petitioner by his action had caused a loss to the tune of U.S. dollar 6,36,000 to the Biman and the State in the matter of acquiring the aircraft for the Biman and obtained for himself or others pecuniary advantage by abusing his official position, Admittedly, the aircraft in question was impounded as a result of a court proceeding initiated by the seller for the alleged breach of contract by the Biman for the purchase of the aircraft. When we asked learned Deputy Attorney General about the result of the court proceeding in London, he could not give us any reply as to the fate or outcome of the court proceeding. Obviously, it appears to me that the Biman did not contest the Court proceeding otherwise there is no plausible reason as to why they should not be aware of its outcome after a lapse of five years. It is not understood nor do I find any plausible reason as to why instead of losing the aircraft permanently the Biman did not pay the balance money and get the aircraft released. Even accepting as true the prosecution case that it was economically a bad deal, the aircraft would have by now more than paid off the price it was acquired for had the Biman got it released by paying the balance money. The prosecution case that the aircraft in question was of inferior quality and defective is belied by the very fact admitted in the F.I.R. that immediately after the purchase the aircraft was put on regular schedule flight of the Biman without any allegation of any break-down. It is interesting to note as asserted by the petitioner in paragraph 24 of his affidavit that the very same aircraft was chartered by the Biman three s ears after in August, 1979 in perfectly air-worthy condition at a cost 15 times higher than what the petitioner had purchased it for in April, 1976. This categorical assertion by the petitioner has not been or could not be controverted by the State. 

 11. The petitioner in his application before this court had alleged malafide. It is difficult to substantiate the allegation of malafide against anybody but certain admitted facts stand out in the instant case which are self-revealing. The agreement in question was signed on 14.4.76 and the petitioner was relieved' of his responsibilities and sent out of the country, on 30.4.76 and the FIR was lodged long after 4 years on 13.5.80 while the petitioner was out of the country. The petitioner returned to Dacca from abroad on 1.7.80 but was again expelled from the country from the Airport on the very same-day at Governmental cost. It is, therefore, not understood as to why the petitioner was not arrested and taken into custody 1.7.80 when a criminal proceeding was already pending against him instead of forcing him out of the country at the cost of public exchequer. As a result of the judgment delivered in the writ petition filed by the petitioner, the petitioner returned to his country on 21.8.81 and the charge sheet in the instant case was submitted on that very date. The petitioner was arrested on the following day and was in custody for 5 days before he was released on bail by an order of the Court. Although the entire transaction leading to the agreement was negotiated by the petitioner along with the Chairman, it was executed and signed by Mr. I4edayet Ahmed, the then Chairman. Biman but according to the prosecution all these were done at the behest and under orders of the petitioner. From the facts revealed in the F.I.R. it was evident that whatever action was taken in the matter was done by the Chairman under his signature. If the petitioner is sought to be prosecuted, it is not understood as to how the Chairman Ms. Hedayet Ahmed could be left out. Instead of being made a co-accused, Mr. Hedayet Ahmed figures as star witness No. 1 for the prosecution. There is an unfortunate trend in our country that whenever there is a change of regime and some corruption and bunglings are unearthed the officers responsible for the same always tried to take shelter behind the plea that they were absolutely innocent and were forced to take those illegal actions under orders or at the behest of the Ministers or the public leaders. Here is a case where a senior civil servant of Mr. Hedayet Ahmed's standing who was holding a very high and responsible position as the Chairman of the Bangladesh Biman wants the world to believe that he was forced to take all these allegedly illegal actions involving millions of dollars in foreign currency under order of the petitioner without ever raising one word of protest. After the fall of the petitioner from power and grace, Mr. Ahmed appears to have made a complete somersault in order to find favour with the persons who had forced the petitioner out of the country It was indeed unfortunate to say the least, that permanent civil servants who are the steel-frame of the Governmental structure should have played into the hands of the designing politicians in their scramble and gamble for power. 

 There is no hard and fast definition of the words used in the statute namely "the abuse of the process of the Court or for ends of justice". The abuse of the process of the court is applied to a. proceeding which is wanting in bonafides and is vexatious and oppressive. The inherent powers of this court are applied for ends of justice when the allegations, even if accepted as true, do not constitute any offence. The learned Deputy Attorney General has argued at length on the question of stifling the prosecution at this stage and had relied on certain authorities on the subject. These authorities are well established and the principles laid down are well settled but the principle must be applied after considering the facts and circumstances of each particular case. He has relied on the cases reported in 19 D.L.R. (S.C.) 439, 19 D.L R. (S.C.) 369, and 31 D.L R. (A.D.) 69. The facts in the aforesaid decisions are clearly distinguishable from the facts of the instant case where not only charge-sheet was submitted but cognizance had also been taken by the court. It must be borne in mind that it took 4 years for the prosecution to make up its mind whether to lodge F.I.R. or not and thereafter it took more than one year and 3 months to submit the charge-sheet. The result of such prolonged and laborious investigation are now before us in the form of F.I.R and the charge-sheet. 

 12. What has emerged are two accusations against the petitioner: firstly, an unauthorised deal, secondly, wrongful gain and consequent loss to the State. So far as the first accusation regarding unauthorised deal is concerned, I have already elaborately dis-cussed it. Even if the accusation is accepted as true, does it constitute a penal offence or does it come within the purview of 'misconduct' as defined in section 5 of Act II of 1947? An act may be improper or even unethical but that does not necessarily make it a criminal act. Secondly, with regard to the accusation of loss and wrongful gain, is there an iota of allegation anywhere either in the F.I.R. or in the charge sheet that the petitioner had obtained any pecuniary advantage for himself or that he had obtained it for others by his action? What has come out of the whole unfortunate transaction is loss to the Biman but the facts revealed clearly go to show that the loss was due to the action taken by the Biman Authorities in refusing to pay the balance amount and not because of any action or decision by the petitioner. Even if it is held that the petitioner was responsible for the loss suffered by the Biman does the law under which he has been charged, contemplate a case of loss as an offence? Even the figure of U.S. dollar 6,36,000 given in the charge-sheet as loss of pecuniary advantage, whatever it may be, is vague and hypothetical. 

 14. It is pertinent to recall that the petitioner was not arrested on 1.7.80 when he landed in Dacca although the instant criminal proceeding was pending against him. Instead, he was expelled from the country. When he returned to the country again as a result of an order of this Court declaring the Government's action in expelling him from the country as illegal, charge-sheet was submitted in this case on that very date and he was arrested the following day. The conclusion, therefore, from the above admitted facts becomes inescapable that the intention of the then Government was to keep him out of the country, failing which, to keep him in custody. A man may be prosecuted for an offence alleged to have been committed but the law does not permit a citizen to be persecuted and harassed. 

 16. I am, therefore, satisfied that no charge under such vague and sweeping allegations can be sustained in a court of law. There is, therefore, no question of stifling the prosecution in a case like this. If the extra ordinary powers of this Court vested under section 561A of the Code of Criminal Procedure cannot be invoked to stop the abuse of the process of Court and for ends of justice and to save a citizen from unnecessary harassment, I do not know in which other circumstances it can be invoked. If a beneficial section such as 561A of the Code is not applied for saving innocent citizens from vexatious proceedings and harassment, then it would be rendered completely nugatory and redundant for all practical purposes. This beneficial and extraordinary powers should be applied not to stifle the prosecution but to stifle any attempt to persecute an innocent citizen and be exercised ex debito justiciae to do real and substantial justice for the administration of which alone the Courts exist. 

 17. Having regard to all these facts and circumstances and my discussions above, I am satisfied that the facts disclosed in the F.I.R. and in the charge sheet do not make out even a prima facie case under section 5(2) of Act II of 1947 and further prolongation of 'the proceedings would only amount to abuse of the process of Court and as such the proceedings are liable to be quashed for ends of justice. 

 In the result, the criminal proceedings pending against the petitioner in Special Case No. 60 of 1981 in the Court of Special Judge, Court No. 1, Dacca Division, Dacca are hereby quashed and the accused-petitioner is discharged from his bail bond forthwith. The Rule is, accordingly, made absolute 

 19. Petitioner Air Vice Marshal (Retired) M.G. Towab, stands accused of an alleged offence under section 5(2) of the Prevention of Corruption Act, 1947 (Act II of 1947) in Special Case No. 60 of 1981 now pending in Court No. 1 of the Special Judge, Dacca Division, Dacca. The petitioner moved this application under section 561 A of the Code of Criminal Procedure and obtained this Rule calling upon the Deputy Commissioner, Dacca to show cause why the aforesaid proceeding should not be quashed. 

 21. It has been alleged in the F.I.R. dated 1.5.80. lodged by the Deputy Director, Bureau of Anti-Corruption, Dacca Division, Dacca (allegations to be noticed in details later on) giving rise to the aforesaid Special Case No. 60 of 1981 that on 14.4.76 the petitioner and the then Chairman Bangladesh Biman unauthorisedly entered into an agreement with PAN AYER, SA, a subsidiary of MIS, Frederick B. Ayer to purchase one Boeing 707-121B aircraft at a cost of U.S. doller 2.365 million. without calling for any tender and quotation in violation of Government decision to purchase 707-320C aircraft, that all the actions taken by the Chairman, Bangladesh Biman in the transaction were reported to have been done under order and direction of the petitioner and that by the aforesaid deal, the petitioner obtained/attempted to obtain pecuniary advantage to the tune of U.S. dollar 6,36,000 either for himself or for others by corrupt or illegal means or by otherwise abusing his official position as a public servant. 

 22. It appears from the petition that on 30.4. 76 the petitioner was arbitrarily relieved of his office and forced out of the country on the same day. He was given a ticket to travel to Munich via London. The petition while abroad sought permission from the Bangladesh Government to return home but his request was not even answered. On 1.7.80, the petitioner however, arrived at the Dacca Airport, but he was not allowed to cross the immigration barrier. He was forcibly put into a Bangkok bound Aircraft and again made to leave the country. The petitioner has stated in his petition that he challenged the illegal and arbitrary action of the Government before this Division in Writ Petitioner 673 of 1980 whereupon it was declared, by judgment and order dated 23.7.81, that the action of the Government was illegal and without lawful authority. The petitioner again came to Dacca in the afternoon of August 21, 81 but on the following morning he was arrested by the police in connection with the aforesaid case and produced before the Chief Metropolitan Magistrate, Dacca. The case record was sent to the Court of Senior Special Judge. Dacca, who by order dated 24.8.81 took cognizence under section 5(2) of Act II of 1947 and then transferred the case to the Court of Mr. Mahbubur Rahman for disposal. The learned Judge upon a prayer made on behalf of the petitioner granted him bail by order dated 27.8.81. This Court while issuing the rule on October 19, 81 stayed all further proceedings of the aforesaid special case. 

 23. The State has appeared to contest the Rule and a counter-affidavit sworn by the Investigating Officer of the case has been filed. It has been asserted, inter alia, in the said counter-affidavit that the action 'of the petitioner as have come to light during investigation have clearly constituted a distinct offence under section 5(2) of Act II of 1947, that the facts in the F.I.R. and in the charge-sheet are based on record and sufficient evidence and that, the prayer of the petitioner is not maintainable on merits because the whole matter had been looked into very thoroughly, extensively and intensively by appropriate-authorities and after being satisfied they had decided to submit charge-sheet in the case for trial. 

 25. Mr. Abdul Malek, the learned Advocate. for the petitioner, has vigorously urged in support of the Rule that upon the facts stated in the F.I.R. and charge-sheet no prima facie case either under section 5(2) of Act II of 1947 or under any other law has been made out which can reasonably go to trial. The learned Advocate has alleged that the facts stated in the and charge-sheet, when considered in the light of the purchase and lease agreements in question, show that , there has been suppression of material facts for the purpose of maligning the petitioner. It has also been argued that there is no pecuniary loss caused to Bangladesh Biman as a result of the purchase agreement as alleged, but loss, if any, was due to the subsequent actions of the authorities of the Biman when the petitioner , was no longer in office. Mr. Malek has also alleged that the delay (about 4 years) in lodging the F.I. R. would show the malafide nature of the proceeding which was taken for a collateral purpose, namely to harass the petitioner. On the aforesaid grounds the learned Advocate has prayed for quashing of the proceeding pending against the petitioner to prevent abuse of the process of the Court and to secure ends of justice. 

 26. The learned Deputy Attorney General has, on the other hand, submitted that since the and charge-sheet disclose a definite, prima facie case against the petitioner the prayer for quashing the proceeding is not legally tenable. He has submitted that it would be against the policy of law to stifle the prosecution at an initial stage, such as in the present case and that the prosecution should be given opportunity to prove its case by adducing evidence at the trial. In support of his submissions he has referred to a number of decisions to which reference will be presently made. 

 27. Before I take up the question for consideration as to whether the proceeding should be quashed or not, it is necessary to see the nature and scope of the inherent power of this court under section 561A of the Cr.P.C. which has been invoked by the petitioner. The authorities on the subject are too numerous and the-law appears to be equally well-settled. The Privy Council, to begin with, in the case of Khwaja Nazir Ahmed reported in AIR 1945 (P.C) 18 declared thus: "It has sometimes been thought that S. 561A has given increased powers to the Court which it did not possess before that section was enacted. But this is not so. The section gives no new powers, it only provides that those which the Court already inherently possess shall be preserved and is inserted, as their Lordships think, lest it should be considered that the only powers possessed by the Court are those expressly conferred by the Criminal Procedure Code and that no inherent power had survived the passing of that Act." 

 28. We are here concerned with the principles for' quashing a criminal proceeding on the ground of preventing 'abuse of process of Court or for securing ends of justice.' The then Supreme Court of Pakistan in the case of M.S. Khawja reported in 17 DLR. (S.C) 153 laid down thus : "Every prosecution for a criminal offence is to be deemed to have been commenced and continued in the public interest, as a duty of the State. It can only be in a very rare case that a superior Court acting under its inherent power to prevent abuse of the process of any Court or otherwise to secure the ends of justice, would deem it appropriate to act so as to place an alleged offence outside the operation of the criminal law, on incidental grounds such as that of dealy or for any reasons other than reasons going to the question whether the allegation is sufficient to constitute an accusation of an offence in law." 

 To quash a judicial proceeding in order to "secure the ends of justice" would involve a finding that if permitted to continue that proceeding would defeat the ends of justice or in other words, would either operate or perpetuate an injustice. To find an "abuse," it should be necessary to see in the proceeding, a perversion of the purpose of the law such as to cause harrassment to an innocent party, to bring about delay, or where no results in furtherance of justice can accrue, and similar perverse results." The Supreme Court again in the case of Raja Haq Nawaz reported in 19 D. L. R. (SC) 369 where the case was at the complaint stage observed that: "Quashment of proceedings at so early a stage gives an unfortunate impression of stifling of criminal prosecutions by exercise of an extra-ordinary power which is given for the dispensation of complete justice, in the forms provided by law. It is necessary that these cases should be examined further, to ensure that the course of even-handed justice has not been prejudiced." 

 Hamoodur Rahman J. has expressed him-self on the subject, in the case of Ghulam Muhammad reported in the same volume (19 DLR (SC) 439), in the following words: "The power given by this section can certainly not be so utilised as to interrupt or divert the ordinary course of criminal procedure as laid down in the procedural statute. The High, Court, as has repeatedly been pointed out in a number of decisions, should be extremely reluctant to interfere in a case where a competent Court has, after examining the evidence adduced before it, came to the view that a prima facie case is disclosed and has framed charges or summoned the accused to appear, unless it can be said that the charge on its face or the evidence, even if believed, does not disclose any offence." Coming nearer home, it will be seen that the Appellate Division of this Court has reiterated the same principles in the case of Bangladesh Tan Khang Hock, reported in 31 D.L.R. (A.D) 69, The Appellate Division while agreeing with the aforesaid principles observed thus: 

 "When exercising this jurisdiction, the High Court would not embark upon an enquiry whether the evidence in question is reliable or not. This is the function of the trial Magistrate and it might so happen that quashment of a criminal proceeding before commencement of trial would amount to stifling the proceeding before the prosecution got an opportunity to bring evidence in support of the accusations. That is why their Lordships of the Judicial Committee in the case of Emperor v. Nazir Ahmad expressed a word of caution that the Court might be acting on treacherous grounds" "in quashing criminal proceedings at the interlocutory stage or at the early stage on the ground that continuation of the proceedings would be an abuse of the process of the Court. We fully agree with the view taken by their Lordships of the Judicial Committee that the extra ordinary power of the Court under section 561A should be exercised very cautiously to avoid miscarriage of justice." 

 29. It is not necessary to draw on further authorities, for, it seems that the principle is well-entrenched that the usual course of the administration of criminal justice in the manner provided by the Cr. P.C. should rarely be interrupted and this court should be extremely reluctant to interfere in a case before the evidence is gone into by the trial court unless it can be said that the allegations, even if are or believed, do not disclose any offence. It is only in very limited cases that upon coming to a finding as to 'abuse of process of Court" or to 'secure ends of justice' as indicated in the cases referred to above that a proceeding may be quashed at an interlocutory stage in exercise of the inherent power of this Court. I shall refer to one more case, from the Indian Jurisdiction, that of R. P. Kapur, reported in AIR 1960 (SC) 866 in which some of the categories of cases have been delineated where the inherent jurisdiction to quash proceedings can and should be exercised. They are: 

 ''(I) Where it manifestly appears that there is a legal bar against the institution or continuance of the criminal proceeding in respect of the offence alleged. Absence of the requisite sanction may, for instance, furnish cases under this category. 

 (II) Where the allegations in the First Information Report or the complaint, even if they are taken at their face value and accepted in their entirety, do not constitute the offence alleged; in such cases no question of appreciating evidence arises; it is a matter merely of looking at the complaint or the First Information Report to decide whether the offence is disclosed or not. 

 (III) Where the allegations made against the accused persons do constitute an offence alleged but there is either no legal evidence adduced in support of the case or the evidence adduced clearly or manifestly fails to prove the charge. In dealing with this class of cases it is important to bear in mind the distinction between a case where there is no legal evidence or where there is evidence which is manifestly and clearly inconsistent with the accusation made and cases where there is legal evidence which on its appreciation may or may not support the accusation in question. In exercising its jurisdiction under S. 51A the High Court would not embark upon an enquiry as to whether the evidence in question is reliable or not. This is the function of the trial magistrate, and ordinarily it would not he open to any party to invoke the High Court's inherent jurisdiction and contend that on a reasonable appreciation of the evidence the accusation made against the accused would not be sustained." 

 30. Keeping the aforesaid principles in view, the only question which is germane for our consideration in the present case is whether the facts stated in the F.I.R. and charge-sheet disclose a prima facie case against the petitioner or not. If they do, this court, on, well-settled principles, must refuse to interfere. If, however, they do not, the finding as to abuse of the process of court' would be irresistible. It is elementary that the facts stated in the F.I.R. or charge-sheet, at this stage, should be presumed to be correct and any assertion contrary there-to cannot be entertained in this proceeding. The Court, it is elementary again, cannot and should not take upon itself the task of resolving issues of facts on affidavits which must be resolved upon evidence to be led before the trial court in accordance with law. It may be that the allegations made against the petitioner are unfounded and/or exaggerated and the contention and assertion of the petitioner are full of substance, even then, this court cannot, again on well-settled principles, turn itself into a trial court and preempt the trial by a process of usurpation of the functions of the trial court. It is only on admitted facts that one has to see whether there is a prima facie case to go to the trial or not. In other words, it will not be permissible to enter into the various questions of fact as has been sought to be raised in the petition and affidavit-in-reply in denial of the allegations made against the petitioner. 

 31. In the present case congnizance has been taken on the basis of a police report, called the charge-sheet Therefore, this is the document to which we must confine ourselves for the time being to find out whether it discloses a prima facie case. It may be mentioned here that the records of the case have not been called for. All the files and documents referred to in the charge-sheet are not before this Court. I have carefully examined both the F.I.R, and charge-sheet. Broadly speaking, the allegation, against the petitioner seems to be that on 14.4.76, he, as a public servant entered into a deal of purchase/lease with a foreign firm in respect of an aircraft (Boeing 707-121-B) for Bangladesh Biman and out of that deal obtained/attempted to obtain for himself or for others pecuniary advantage to the tune of U.S. dollar 6,36,00 Let me now examine the facts a little more closely. In the first place, it has been stated in the charge-sheet that in September, 1975 Bangladesh Biman submitted a proposal to the Planning Commission through the Government for acquiring a 'Boeing 707-320-C aircraft at a cost of U S. dollar 5.3 million. The Planning Commission and the Government approved of the proposal in principle but without receiving the requisite formal sanction the petitioner unauthorisedly negotiated with a firm to purchase a different type of aircraft. Next, it has been alleged that the petitioner dishonestly came in contact with PANAYER S.A. a subsidiary of M/S. Frederick B. Ayer and on 14.4.76 compelled the then Chairman Bangladesh Biman to execute an agreement for purchasing one Boeing 707-121-B aircraft at U.S. dollar 2.365 million without calling for any tender or quotation in deliberate violation of Government order to acquire one Boeing 707 320C aircraft. In terms of this agreement, Biman had the option to select one out of three aircrafts of the same series to be made available within eight weeks. The petitioner got the agreement executed and fixed the price without getting any of the aircrafts, which were all second hand, examined by any technical expert. One of the aforesaid aircrafts was offered to PIA at U.S dollar 2.1 million on 16.3.76 but the HA rejected it considering the same to be unfavourable. On the same date, the petitioner got a lease agreement executed between Biman and the same firm for lease of a Boeing (707-121-B) aircraft (serial No.17903) for the interim period of eight weeks on rent-free basis. It has been alleged that this aircraft was inferior and defective one. 

 34. What I have reproduced above are all allegations repeat, mere allegations and each one of the items of allegation has to be established by legal evidence before the petitioner can be found guilty of the offence alleged. But taking the allegations as they are I have found it difficult to hold that they do not make out a prima facie case against the petitioner. Shorn of the details, the moot question will be whether the deal in respect of the aircraft in question was entered into by the petitioner with an ulterior motive to gain pecuniary advantage either for himself or for others or whether it was an honest transaction in the best interest of the Biman and the country. I have carefully gone through the petitioner's assertions made in the petition and in the affidavit-in-reply giving the whole background and perspective of the disputed transaction and denying the allegations made in the F.I.R. and charge-sheet. I am conscious that the petitioner was not a small official of the Govt. but he was, so to say, a leader of the then Government. Besides, he is undoubtedly a highly qualified and experienced person in the field of aviation. Viewed in this context, the facts which have been asserted by the petitioner in, defence of his actions, if properly brought on record, are entitled to the highest consideration by any court of the first instance where allegations such as above are made and sought to be established against him: But this we cannot do in this proceeding and must leave it to the trial court in adherence to the principles referred to above. 

 35. The learned Advocate for the petitioner has argued upon recounting the background of initiating the present proceeding against the petitioner that it was started with malafide intention to harass the petitioner. In this connection he has particularly drawn our attention to the fact of long delay in lodging the F.I.R. We have also noticed the Government's dealing with the petitioner before the present case was taken to the Court. Obviously those matters were of political nature and related to high policy pursued by the Government of the day. Those matters are not before us in this proceeding and in the determination of the truth or otherwise of the allegations made in the criminal case they are not, in my opinion, quite relevant. As far as the question of delay is concerned it is now well-settled that limitation does not apply to criminal proceedings and it is also in appropriate to examine the question of delay through the actions of the Government, or the prosecution authorities, as if they gave rise to equities on the same footing as in a civil matter interprets [reference 17 DLR (SC) 153]. As far as malafides or oblique motive of the Government is concerned, it will suffice to say that if the prosecution can prove the offence alleged by adducing legal evidence then the question of motive behind initiating the prosecution would not be relevant. 

 36. The learned Advocate for the petitioner sought to argue that the loss, if any, sustained. Biman in the aircraft deal in question was due to the subsequent unilateral and unwise action of the authorities of the Biman when the petitioner was no longer in the picture and as such the petitioner could not be held responsible for such loss. I have already noticed that the petitioner has raised many other formidable facts in this affidavit-in-reply which have the effect of exonerating him from the offence alleged. The learned Advocate for the petitioner submitted before us that if the purchase/lease documents were examined it would be found that the Investigating Officer suppressed material facts in the F.I.R. and charge-sheet in order to implicate and malign the petitioner. Now all these documents would involve examination of evidence; both oral and documentary, which, I have already held, cannot be undertaken in this proceedings. In view of the special facts of this case I have taken pains to point out the difficulty and the legal position for which this court cannot and should not embark upon examining the myriad facts which have been alleged by the petitioner nor can we ask the prosecution to lead evidence before us. Having given my anxious consideration to the contents of the charge-sheet I have found it difficulty to hold that it was merely a command performance without any real investigation in the matter. The Investigating Officer has stated on oath before this Court that the Government referred the matter to the then Co-Ordination & Control Cell for National Security in the middle of 1979. Accordingly, the Officers of the Co-Ordination and Control Cell for National Security held preliminary enquiries by visiting different countries and submitted report which was considered at the highest Govt. level which took a decision to refer the matter to the Bureau of Anti-Corruption in April, 1980 for taking necessary action as per law. Thereafter, the case was started/investigated duly by the Bureau of Anti-Corruption. 

 37. Thus having regard to the facts and circumstances of the case and in view of the foregoing discussion, I have come to the conclusion that this is not a case in which the proceeding can be lawfully quashed at this stage. I want to make it clear, however, that my conclusion here must not prejudice the petitioner in any manner at the trial which should be fairly held in accordance with law. 

 This reference under section 429 Cr. P.C. has arisen as a result of the difference in opinion between the two Judges of this court in a Rule under section 561A Cr.P.C. for quashing the criminal proceeding in Special Case No. 60 of 1981 under section 5(2) of the Prevention of Corruption Act, 1947 (Act II of 1947) pending in the court of Mr. Mahbubur Rahman, Special Judge, Court No. 1, Dacca. Mr. M. A. Hossain, Senior Special Judge, Dacca on 24.8.81 on receipt of the F.I.R., charge-sheet and other connected papers took cognizance of the case under Act II of 1947 and transferred the said case to Mr. Mahbubur Rahman, Special Judge, Court No. 1, for disposal. According to the accused petitioner he was released on bail by the Special Judge, Court No. 1, Dacca Division on 27.8.81. 

 2. The facts of the case are that Mr. Md. Altaf Hossain, Deputy Director, Bureau of Anti-Corruption, Dacca Division, Dacca lodged a F.I.R. on 13.5.80 at P.S. Ramna, Dacca against the accused petitioner Air Vice-Marshal (Rtd.) M.G. Tawab under section 5(2) of Act II of 1947. The said Deputy Director, Bureau of Anti-Corruption submitted charge-sheet against the accused petitioner on 21.8.81 under section 5(2) of Act II of 1947 citing 35 witnesses and submitting a list of 19 documents. The case for the prosecution, as it appears from the F.I.R. and charge-sheet, in brief is that the accused petitioner A.V.M. (Rtd.) M. G. Tawab, was at the time of occurrence the Deputy Chief Martial Law Administrator in charge of some Ministries including the Ministry of Civil Aviation of the Government of Bangladesh. In September, 1975 Bangladesh Biman which is attached to the Ministry of Civil Aviation submitted a proposal to the Planning Commission through the Ministry of Civil Aviation for acquiring a Boeing 707-320C air-craft at a cost of U.S. dollar 5.3 million. The proposal was approved by the Planning Commission and the Government in principle. Without receiving any formal sanction order in this respect the accused petitioner without any authorisation from the Government negotiated with a firm in January, 1976 to purchase a Boeing 720B second-hand aircraft and settled its price. But the deal could not be materialised due to the timely intervention of the Government. In 1974 a firm named M/S. Frederick B Ayer offered to sell a Boeing 707-1388 air craft bearing Manufacturer's Serial No. 17697 at U.S. dollar 2.4 million but the Bangladesh Biman did not accept the offer as its experts considered it to be unfavourable and uneconomical. In spite of this in March 1976 the accused petitioner with dishonest motive got in touch with the said firm and himself led a team to London and inspected the said second-hand aircraft at Stansted Airport on 28.3.76. But this time also the team considered it unsuitable on various grounds. Having failed to purchase the aforesaid aircraft from M/S. Frederick B. Ayer due to unfavourable report by Biman's experts, the petitioner again with dishonest intention contacted PANAYER S.A., a subsidiary of aforesaid M/S. Frederick B. Ayer and on 14.4.76 without any approval of the Ministry of Finance, without authorisation of the Government, without calling for any tender and without obtaining any technical report by the technical experts of the Bangladesh Biman compelled Mr. Hedayet Ahmed. the then Chairman, Bangladesh Biman to execute an agreement for purchasing one Boeing 707-121B at the price of U.S. dollar 2.365 million which was also in deliberate violation of Government's decision to purchase the Boeing 707-320-C aircraft. In terms of this agreement Bangladesh Biman was to select one out of three second-hand aircrafts of the same series bearing Manufacturer's serial Nos.17587,17590 and 17591 to be made available within 8 weeks. One of these three aircrafts was offered by the said company to P.I.A. at a price of U.S. dollar 21. million on 16.3.76 but the P.I.A had rejected it considering it to be unfavorable. On the same day i.e. 14.4.76 the accused petitioner got a lease agreement executed between the Bangladesh Biman and the said firm for a lease of a Boeing 707-121-B aircraft, bearing Manufacturer's serial No. 17903 and U.S. Registration No. N.778 for the interim period of 8 weeks on a rent free basis on the condition that by that time, the so-called purchased aircraft would be made available to Bangladesh Biman. This aircraft bearing Manufacturer's serial No. 17903, according to the prosecution, was also inferior and a defective one. According to the terms and conditions of the aforesaid purchase agreement, 40% of the price amounting to U.S dollar 9,46,000/- was to be paid in cash at the time of delivery of the leased aircraft and the balance of 60% amounting to U.S. dollar 14,19,000/- was to be paid by Bangladesh Biman by opening an irrecoverable letter of credit in favour of the seller firm with the First National Bank of Boston in London and that amount was to be released upon presentation by the Seller firm of a bill of sale together with a delivery receipt for the aircraft duly signed by the Chairman, Bangladesh Biman who came to London under the order of the accused petitioner who also signed each of the pages of both the deeds of purchase and lease and himself carried out the negotiations to conclude the deals. On the same day, i. e. on 14.4.76 the accused petitioner got a blank delivery receipt signed by Mr. Hedayet Ahmed, the then Chairman, Bangladesh Biman and the said blank delivery receipt was handed over to the aforesaid seller firm. The accused petitioner did not allow the Bangladesh Biman to call for an international tender. Accused petitioner himself decided to buy one of the aforesaid aircraft and did not deliberately ask the technical experts of Bangladesh Biman to give a technical report. The accused petitioner himself fixed the price with the Seller Company much above the market price and did not allow the Chairman, Bangladesh Biman and the Secretary, Ministry of Civil Aviation to obtain the sanction and approval of the Ministry of Finance headed by another Deputy. Chief Martial Law Administrator (namely, Lt. General Ziaur Rahman) and of the Government before finalizing the deal and executing both the deeds of purchase and lease and signing a blank delivery receipt. Contravening rule 10 of the Rules of Business, 1975 the accused petitioner dishonestly and deliberately avoided taking prior authorization and concurrence of the Ministry of Finance (headed by the said Deputy Chief Martial Law Administrator) and of the Government before finalising the deal, signing the deeds of purchase and lease and signing the blank deli-very receipt as the Ministry of Finance and the Government would have raised the inconvenient and unpalatable questions of selection of model, calling for international tender, even if calling for international tender was exempted by the Government, the question of examining the terms and conditions of various offers from a number of firms, and technical condition of those aircrafts and after obtaining report of the technical experts of the Bangladesh Biman the matter would be examined and scrutinised by the Ministry of Finance and the Government before giving sanction and approval for finalising the deal of purchase of a selected aircraft at a stipulated price. At the time of ferrying the aircraft from Stansted to Heathrow Airport on 16.4.76 Captain Mashiur Rahman of Bangladesh Biman detected a number of faults in the leased aircraft and refused to accept it but he was compelled by the accused petitioner to accept it. The down payment of 40% of the stipulated price was paid at the instance of the accused petitioner in cash at the time of delivery of the leased aircraft. The aircraft was put in Biman's scheduled flight on 17.4.76 when also the Captain detected several faults in the aircraft. On the date of executing the purchase and the lease deed i.e. on 14 4.76 the accused petitioner stealthily confirmed in writing to the Seller Firm to purchase the leased aircraft provided the firm would obtain its title though the accused petitioner knew that it was of inferior quality. On 22.4.76 the seller firm requested the Chairman, Bangladesh Biman to have the purchase agreement amended so that the Biman would have no option but to purchase the leased aircraft. Although the earlier agreement signed by the Chairman, Bangladesh Biman was to purchase one of the three aircrafts bearing Manufacturer's No. 17587, 17590 and 15591, the seller firm filled the blank delivery receipt showing therein the particulars of the leased aircraft bearing Manufacturer's No. 17903 which, according to the prosecution, shows why the accused petitioner dishonestly got the blank delivery receipt signed by the Chairman, Bangladesh Biman. The Seller Company presented the filled in delivery receipt along with other connected papers and demanded the payment of balance 60% of the stipulated amount of U S. dollar 14,19,000/- from the Sonali Bank, London. Detecting the fraudulent transaction the Bangladesh Biman and the Sonali Bank intervened and did not pay the balance amount of U.S. dollar i ,4 t 9,000/- when Bangladesh Biman had sent the leased aircraft for maintenance repair to London on 10 5.76. On 10.5.76 the Seller Company. i.e. PAN AYER got the said aircraft impounded through Court on the ground of non-payment of the balance amount of U.S. dollar 1,4,19,000/. It appears that the Bangladesh Biman had recovered U.S. dollars 3,10,000/- by putting the said aircraft on its scheduled flights from 17.4.76 till 10.5.76. The accused petitioner thus dishonestly obtained an undue pecuniary advantage either for the seller company or for himself or for any other person to the tune of U.S. dollar 6,36,000/-: and also attempted to obtain either for himself or for others pecuniary advantage from the aforesaid deal of purchase of an aircraft at a price which was much higher than its market price by corrupt or illegal means or by otherwise abusing his position as a public servant. The accused petitioner was relieved of his duties by the Chief Martial Law Administrator on 30.6.76. He was allowed to travel to Munich where his German wife and children used to reside and where he used to carry on his business The Government referred the matter to the Co-ordination and Control Cell for National Security. Accordingly the officers of the Co-ordination and Control Cell for National Security held preliminary enquiries by visiting different countries and submitted report which was considered by the Government at its highest level. The Government then referred the matter to the Bureau of Anti-Corruption in April, 1980 for taking necessary action in accordance with law. As already stated the aforesaid Officer of the Bureau of Anti-Corruption lodged the F.I.R and after investigating the case submitted charge- sheet (Annexure `B') on 21.8 81. On 19.10.81 the accused-petitioner obtained this. Rule and further proceeding of the said special case was stayed till the disposal of the Rule. 

 The prosecution has denied this allegation as baseless by filing a counter affidavit The delay in lodging the F.I.R. has been explained by the prosecution by stating that previous to the lodging of the F.I.R. the whole matter in respect of this case was enquired into thoroughly, extensively and intensively by the Government through its appropriate agencies and after the Government was satisfied on the basis of this enquiry, the F.I.R was lodged bonafide. The prosecution has further stated that after a thorough investigation the Investigating Officer duly submitted charge-sheet citing a number of witnesses and submitted a list of documents. Mr. Sohrab Ali, the learned Deputy Attorney General, appearing on behalf of the State submits that the F.I.R. was lodged and the charge-sheet was submitted against the accused petitioner in the public interest and that there is no truth in the allegation that the prosecution was started for any co-lateral purpose or with any malafide motive. 

 4. There is no denying of the fact that if the prosecution case as given out in the F.I.R. and the charge-sheet is believed that the accused petitioner by corrupt or illegal means or by otherwise abusing his position as a public servant dishonestly obtained and attempted to obtain for himself or for any other person or persons a pecuniary advantage from the aforesaid deal of purchase of an aircraft from the seller Company, he is guilty of committing the offence of 'criminal misconduct' as defined in section 5(1) (d) of the Prevention of Corruption Act, 1947. There-fore, it cannot be said. that this Court should interfere under section 561A Cr.P.C. on the ground that even if the allegations made by the prosecution are accepted as true, they do not disclose any criminal offence against the accused petitioner. It also cannot be said that it is a case which has no evidence to support the allegation made by the prosecution. The accused petitioner in his petition and the affidavit-in-reply has alleged various facts and has given various arguments in his defence and has tried to show that he is innocent and the action taken by him are bonafide. At the time of trial the accused petitioner will have enough opportunity to try to establish his defence version of the case. This court in exercise of its power under section 561A Cr.P.C. cannot embark upon an enquiry to determine the guilt or innocence of the accused petitioner. 

 6. The learned Deputy Attorney General refers to the judgment of my learned brother Abdur Rahman Chowdhury, J. and point out that the learned Judge Misconceived the prosecution case by stating that the gist of prosecution case was that firstly, the accused petitioner made the purchase of the aircraft in question without authorisation of the Government and that secondly, the impounding of the aircraft by the seller Company through the Court had caused loss to the Biman and the Government to the tune of U.S. dollar 6,36,000/-. He submitted that the gist of the prosecution case is that the accused petitioner by corrupt or illegal means, by otherwise abusing his position as public servant dishonestly obtained or attempted to obtain for himself or for any other persons a pecuniary advantage by making Bangladesh Biman to execute a deed of purchase of an aircraft from the Seller Company. There is substance in this argument. Had it been simply a case of making the Bangladesh Biman enter into an agreement of purchase from the Seller Company an aircraft without any authorisation from the Government and causing a financial loss to the Bangladesh Biman and the Government due to impounding of the aircraft by the Seller Company through the Court, it would disclose no offence of 'criminal misconduct' as defined in section 5(1)(d) of the Prevention of Corruption Act, 1947 or any other offence under any law. The offence allegedly committed by the accused petitioner is that he by corrupt or illegal means or otherwise by abusing his position as a public servant dishonestly obtained or attempted to obtain for himself or for any other person or persons a pecuniary advantage from the deal of purchase of an aircraft from the Seller Company. 

 "It is not understood nor do I find any plausible reason as to why instead of losing the aircraft permanently the Biman did not pay the balance money and get the aircraft released. Even accepting as true the prosecution case that it was economically a bad deal. the aircraft would have by now more than paid off the price it was acquired for, had the Biman got it released by paying the balance money, The prosecution case that the aircraft in question was of inferior quality and defective is belied by the very fact admitted in the F.I.R that immediately after the purchase the air-craft was put on regular schedule flight of the Biman without any allegation of any break-down. It is interesting to note as asserted by the petitioner in paragraph 24 of his affidavit-in-reply that the very same aircraft was chartered by the Biman three years after in August, 1979 in perfectly air-worthy condition at a cost 15 times higher than what the petitioner had purchased it for in April; 1976." 

 If the accused by corrupt or illegal means or by otherwise abusing his position as public servant dishonestly obtained or attempted to obtain for himself or for any other person or persons a pecuniary advantage by making the Bangladesh Biman enter into a deal of a purchase of an aircraft from the Seller Company, then the argument is of no avail to the accused that the entire amount of the dishonestly stipulated price would have been sufficiently paid off and realised by operating the aircraft for a certain period by Bangladesh Biman if it had paid the remaining 60% of the stipulated price. It is common sense that a criminal offence is complete if an accused accepts the illegal gratification or by corrupt or illegal means or by otherwise abusing his position as public servant dishonestly obtains or attempts to obtain for himself or for any other person or persons a pecuniary advantage from a deal of purchase and the argument that if the balance amount of the stipulated price was paid, the purchaser Bangladesh Biman would have re-covered the entire amount within a certain period of time does not save the accused from the charge of committing a criminal offence. If the prosecution proves or the accused admits the charge that the accused purchased for U.S. dollar 2.3 million an aircraft which was available in the market for, say, U.S. dollar 2 million dishonestly obtaining pecuniary advantage either for himself or for someone else by corrupt or illegal means or by otherwise abusing his position as public servant, he has clearly committed the offence of “criminal misconduct" as defined in section 5(1) (d) of Act II of 1947 even if its found that the said inflated price paid by the public servant dishonestly would have nevertheless been recovered even with some profit if the said air craft was duly operated commercially for a certain period of time. Further, the mere fact that after taking delivery the leased aircraft bearing Manufacturer's Serial No. 1703 operated by Bangladesh Biman on its schedule flight upto 10.5.76 when it  was sent to London for maintenance repair does not at all show in any way from the technical point of view that the aircraft which was a second-hand one was not of inferior quality and was not defective which was presumably the reason for which the Bangladesh Biman could not buy after obtaining approval by the Government by paying the balance amount of 60% of the stipulated price. In paragraph 24 of the affidavit-in-reply the petitioner has alleged as follows:— 

 In exercise of the power under section .561A Cr. P.C. this Court cannot convert itself into a trial Court and embark upon an inquiry to find out the veracity of various such new statements made by the accused in an affidavit-in-reply. Further even if it was true that the same aircraft was chartered by Bangladesh Biman at a such higher rate than the petitioner had negotiated for three years later, this does not save him from the charge of Committing the offence of criminal misconduct' as defined in section (5)(1)(d) of Act It of 1947 as alleged by the prosecution and even if such statement is true, one might find that the price of chartering such aircraft might have gone up as the international prices had gone up and that the owner company might have invested huge amounts for replacing the various 'old and worn out parts, components and systems of the said aircraft. 

 "Although the entire transaction leading to the agreement was negotiated by the petitioner along with the Chairman. it was executed and signed by Mr. Hedayet Ahmed, the then Chairman, Biman but according to the prosecution all these were done at the behest and under orders of the petitioner. From the facts revealed  in the F:I.R. it was evident that whatever action was taken in the matter was done by the Chairman under his signature. If the petitioner is sought to be prosecuted, it is not understood, as to how the Chairman, Mr. Hedayet Ahmed could be left out. Instead of being made a co-accused, Mr. Hedayet Ahmed figures as star witness. No. 1 for the prosecution Here is a case where a Senior Civil Servant of Hedayet Ahmed's standing who was holding a very high and responsible position as the Chairman of the Bangladesh Biman wants the world to believe that he was forced to take all these allegedly illegal actions involving millions of dollars in foreign currency under orders of petitioner without ever raising one word of protest. After the fall of the petitioner from power and grace. Mr. Ahmed appears to have made a complete somersault in order to find favour with the persons who had forced the petitioner out of the country." 

 It is the prosecution case that the accused petitioner dishonestly got in touch with the Seller Company, himself selected certain inferior quality aircrafts being Boeing 707-121B in contravention of Government's prior decision in principle to acquire a Boeing 707-320C at a cost of U.S. dollar 5:3 million, himself settled the price with the Seller Company at U.S. dollar 2.365 millions and himself put his signatures on each page of the two deeds of purchase and lease and Mr. Hedayet Ahmed, Chairman of Bangladesh Biman had to sign the said deeds of purchase and lease and the blank delivery receipt under the order of the petitioner who was his immediate superior authority. In the affidavit-in-reply it has been stated on behalf of the accused petitioner in Sub-paragraphs (f), (h) and (j) of paragraph 14 as follows: 

 10. It has been argued by the petitioner that no undue pecuniary advantage was obtained by the accused petitioner dishonestly either for himself or for any one else from the aforesaid deal of purchase of aircraft from the Seller Company. This question of dishonestly obtaining or dishonestly attempting to obtain either for the petitioner him-self or for any other person by corrupt or illegal means or by otherwise abusing his position as public servant is to be determined at the trial on the basis of the evidence, facts and circumstances on record. At this stage it can merely be said that the prosecution case as alleged in the F.I.R. and the charge-sheet prima facie discloses an offence of criminal misconduct against the accused petitioner as defined in section 5(l)(d) of Act II of 1947 and that from the charge-sheet submitted by the prosecution it cannot be said that it is a case of no evidence. The learned Deputy Attorney General has referred to the decision in the case of M. S. Khawaja vs. State 17 D.L.R. (S.C.) 153 wherein it has been observed: 

 "Limitation does not apply to criminal prosecution arid it is also inappropriate to examine questions of delay through the actions of the Government or the prop section authorities, as if they gave rise to equities, on the same footing as in a civil matter inter pastes. Every prosecution for a criminal offence is to be deemed to have been commenced and continued in the public interest, as a duty of State. It can only be in a very rare case that a superior Court acting under its inherent power "to prevent abuse of the process of any Court or otherwise to secure the ends of justice" would deem it appropriate to act so as to place an alleged offence outside the operation of the criminal law on incidental grounds such as that of delay, or for any reasons other than reasons going to the question whether the allegation is sufficient to constitute an accusation of an offence in law" 

 11. The learned Deputy Attorney General also refers to the decision in the case of Abdul Quader Vs. State, 28 D.L.R. (A.D) 38 wherein it has been observed: 

 "The exercise of this jurisdiction (under section 561A Cr.P.C.) will depend upon the facts and circumstances of each case. Interference even at an initial stage may be justified where the facts are so preposterous that even on the admitted facts no case can stand against the accused and that a further prolongation of the prosecution would amount to harassment to an innocent party and abuse of the process of the Court……………If the criminal proceedings in question is in respect of an offence alleged to have been committed by an accused person and it manifestly appears that there is a legal bar against' the institution or continuance of the said proceedings, the High Court would be justified in quashing the proceedings on that ground. Cases may also wise where ' the allegations in the First Information Report or the complaint even if they are taken at their face value and accepted in their entirety, do not constitute the offence alleged. In such cases no question of appreciating evidence arises, it is a matter merely of looking at the complaint or the First Information Report to decide whether the offence alleged is disclosed or not. In such cases it would be legitimate for the High Court to hold that it would be manifestly unjust to allow process of the criminal Court to be issued against the person..........In exercising the jurisdiction under section 561A Cr.P.C. the Court would not embark upon an enquiry as to whether the evidence in question is reliable or not.. That is the function of the trial Magistrate and ordinarily it would not be open to any party to invoke the High Court's inherent jurisdiction and contend that on a reasonable appreciation of the evidence the accusation made against the accused would not be sustained." 

 12. In the cases of Sheikh Mujibur .Rahman and another Vs. The State (1963) 15 DLR 549 ; P.L.D. 1964 Dacca 330; Nazir Kassab, Shah Vs. The State, (1965) 17 DLR (SC) 26; P.L.D. 1965 (S.C.) and Jamdhar Khan Vs. The State, 27 D.L.R. (A.D) 35 it has been held that where the accused has ceased to be a public servant at the time the court took cognizance of the offence, no sanction is required. So the bar to prosecution of the accused petitioner without the sanction of the Government as contemplated in section 6(5) of Criminal Law Amendment Act, 1958 has no application in this case as the accused has ceased to be a public servant at the time the Senior Special Judge, Dacca took cognizance of the offence. 

 13. The learned Deputy Attorney General submits that the said sub-paragraphs (2) and (3) of paragraph 3A of the Fourth Schedule of the suspended Constitution as amended by the Proclamations (Amendment) Order, 1977 dated 23rd April, 19 a has no application whatsoever in the present case as commission of any criminal offence such as the offence of the criminal misconduct by corrupt or illegal means or by abusing his position as a public servant by dishonestly obtaining undue pecuniary advantage either for himself or for any other person or taking illegal gratification or committing criminal breach of trust, etc. is not protected by this provision. There is substance in this submission of the learned Deputy Attorney General. If at the trial it is proved by the prosecution that the accused petitioner committed the offence of criminal misconduct by dishonestly obtaining undue pecuniary advantage either for himself or for anyone else by corrupt or illegal means or otherwise abusing his position as public servant or committed the offence of taking illegal gratification etc. the mere fact that he was one of the Deputy Chief Martial Law Administrators at the time of the commission of such offence will not bring his criminal acts within purview of sub-paragraphs (2) and (3) of paragraph 3A of the Fourth Schedule of the suspended Constitution as amended by the Proclamations (Amendment) Order, 1977 dated 23rd April, 1977. 

 14. Before parting with this case I should observe that many accused persons in this country do not understand the limited scope of the inherent power of this Court under section 561A Cr.P.C. and very often compel their lawyers to come up with these petitions with the hope that this Court will go beyond the F.I.R. and the charge-sheet and accept the defence version of the case ex parte and quash the criminal proceedings pending against them. I could not but agree more with my learned brother A. T. M. Afzal, J. when he says, "I have taken pains to point out the difficulty and the legal position far which this court cannot and should not embark upon examining the myriad of facts which have been alleged by the petitioner nor can we ask the prosecution to lead evidence before us." 

 In the result, the Rule is discharged. The order staying further proceedings in Special Case No. 60 of 1981 is vacated. The learned Special Judge is directed to hold and finish the trial as expeditiously as possible.
